chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, and Muhammad ibn Abi Abdullah, from Isḥāq ibn Muḥammad, from Ḥarz ibn Muḥammad, who said:
I wrote to Abū Muḥammad (peace be upon him), 'Why did Allāh obligate fasting?' So the answer came: 'So that the rich may experience the pangs of hunger, and thus feel compassion for the poor.'

key_terms.يَحِنَّ: To feel compassion / To yearn with mercy

ai.seo_question: What is the wisdom behind the obligation of fasting in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Recorded in al-Kafi, this hadith from Imam al-Mahdi (or Imam al-Hadi, depending on the specific chain interpretation of Abi Muhammad) elucidates the pedagogical wisdom of fasting as a mechanism for social empathy. It emphasizes that the physical deprivation of the wealthy is not merely ritualistic but serves to bridge the experiential gap with the poor, fostering genuine compassion (ḥinn) and motivating charitable action.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Muhammad, and Muhammad Bin Abu Abdullah, from Is’haq Bin Muhammad, from Hamza Bin Muhammad who said,

‘I wrote to Abu Muhammad<sup>asws</sup>, ‘Why did Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Obligate the Fasting?’ So the answer came: ‘In order for the rich one to experience the pangs of huger so that he would be compassionate upon the poor’.
en.sarwar: 6. Ali ibn Muhammad and Muhammad ibn abu ‘Abd Allah has narrated from Ishaq ibn Muhammad from Hamzah ibn Muhammad who has said the following: “

I once wrote to abu Muhammad, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, and asked, ‘Why has Allah made fasting obligatory?’ The answer was, ‘It is made obligatory so that affluent people can feel the taste of hunger and become compassionate to the poor.’”
